seo_title: Jersey Devil: Mother Leeds, the 1909 panic and the real origin
seo_desc: Where the Jersey Devil legend actually comes from, including the Leeds family and Benjamin Franklin's almanac feud, the week in January 1909 when New Jersey panicked, and what the Pine Barrens look like today.
summary: A hooved, winged devil said to haunt the New Jersey Pine Barrens since 1735, with a stranger origin than the story admits and one very loud week in 1909.
body: The Jersey Devil is the monster of the Pine Barrens, the big stretch of pine and cedar swamp in southern New Jersey. The usual description is a horse or goat head, bat wings, clawed hands, cloven hooves and a forked tail, and a scream that people describe the same way every time.

The famous story says Mother Leeds cursed her 13th child in 1735 and it turned into a devil that flew up the chimney. The less famous story is that the name started as colonial politics and a newspaper feud, and the creature as we picture it only settled into shape after a week of mass panic in January 1909.
No killings, no body and no photograph of the Jersey Devil have ever been documented. What's real is the 1909 wave, the newspaper record, and a legend that generated an NHL team name.

sections.h: Mother Leeds and the thirteenth child
p: The popular version goes like this. A woman named Leeds in the Pine Barrens already had twelve children. When she found out she was pregnant with a thirteenth she cursed it out loud, saying let this one be the devil. The baby arrived looking normal and then changed, growing wings, hooves, a tail and claws, and it beat the room with its tail before flying up the chimney and out into the pines.

Nobody agrees on the year. 1735 is the one you see most, but versions put it at Leeds Point, at Burlington, or in a story set near Mays Landing around 1855 where a Mrs. Leeds wished a stork would bring her a devil instead of a baby and got one.

There is a real family behind it. Deborah Leeds and her husband Japhet Leeds lived at Leeds Point, and Japhet's 1736 will names twelve children, which lines up too neatly with the story for people to ignore. Whether that's the seed of the legend or a coincidence is another question.

sections.h: The part with Benjamin Franklin in it
p: Brian Regal, a historian of science at Kean University, went digging and came up with a much stranger origin than a cursed baby, and his version explains why the creature looks the way it does.

Daniel Leeds was a surveyor and almanac publisher in colonial New Jersey who got on the wrong side of the local Quakers. He printed astrological material in his almanacs, which his congregation decided was pagan, and the books were censored and destroyed. He didn't back down. He kept printing, converted to Anglicanism, wrote anti-Quaker tracts and sided with the royal governor, and in 1700 the Burlington Meeting answered with a pamphlet called Satan's Harbinger Encountered that accused him of working for the devil.

His son Titan Leeds inherited the almanac business, which put him in direct competition with Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack. In 1733 Franklin jokingly predicted in print that Titan Leeds would die that October. Leeds was furious and called Franklin a fool and a liar in public, and Franklin answered by insisting Leeds really had died and that the surviving almanacs must be written by his ghost. He kept calling him a ghost even after Leeds actually died in 1738.

On top of all that, the Leeds family crest carried a wyvern, a two-legged dragon with bat wings. Regal's read is that a family the neighbours already saw as political and religious outcasts, with a dragon on the letterhead and a running public feud with Franklin, turned into the Leeds Devil in local gossip. The devil name shows up in print as Leeds Devil or Devil of Leeds long before anyone writes Jersey Devil.

sections.h: The week New Jersey lost its mind, January 1909
p: For the week of January 16 to 23, 1909, newspapers across South Jersey and Philadelphia ran hundreds of reports. It seems to have started with strange tracks in the snow and then snowballed, because soon people were seeing the thing itself all over South Jersey, and in Delaware and western Maryland too.

The reports from that week are the good stuff. The creature attacked a trolley car in Haddon Heights. It turned up at a social club in Camden. Police in Camden and in Bristol, Pennsylvania fired at it and hit nothing. Schools closed, workers stayed home, and armed groups of hunters and vigilantes went out into the pines to find it.

The Philadelphia Zoo reportedly offered $10,000 for the creature, which brought out the hoaxers, including one that still makes me laugh, a kangaroo fitted with fake claws and bat wings. That is the level of craft the Jersey Devil inspired in 1909.

sections.h: Bonaparte, Decatur and the other stories
p: Once a legend gets going, famous names attach themselves to it. Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon's older brother, is said to have seen the Jersey Devil while hunting on his estate at Bordentown around 1820. Commodore Stephen Decatur supposedly saw a flying creature at the Hanover Mill Works, fired a cannonball at it and hit nothing. Neither story comes with anything you could call evidence.

There are other reports scattered through the record. Livestock killings blamed on the devil in 1840, more in 1841 with tracks and screams, a Greenwich Township farmer in 1925 who shot something after it went for his chickens and photographed the body, and a Downingtown, Pennsylvania animal with red eyes in 1937 that a reporter compared to the Jersey Devil. In 1960 the merchants around Camden offered $10,000 for capture and said they'd build a zoo for it. Nobody ever produced the animal.

The name also went national in a way the Pine Barrens didn't. When the NHL's Colorado Rockies moved east in 1982 the franchise became the New Jersey Devils, which means the state's hockey team is named after a monster that may have started as an insult about a surveyor's family.

Most of the explanations are about people rather than animals. The Pine Barrens were the kind of place outsiders were told not to go, full of pine robbers, deserters and people living outside the rules, and locals had reasons to keep the reputation going. Two early 20th century eugenics studies made things worse by describing Barrens residents as criminals and defectives, research that is now considered biased, unscientific and probably falsified.

Misidentified animals do the rest of the work. A big owl, a heron, a deer breaking cover, a horse with a strange gait in bad light, and a scream from a fox or a screech owl that sounds like a woman in trouble. Once the picture of a winged horse-headed devil got into the papers in 1909, every odd thing in the pines became it.
For the record, I love the legend. I just don't think there's an animal. There's a swamp with a reputation, a family name, a newspaper war and a very good panic.

Leeds Point up in Atlantic County is the place the story is anchored, and there's a small monument and a general store that leans into it. The Pine Barrens themselves are enormous, over a million acres of pine and cedar, and the Batsto Village historic site and Wharton State Forest are the easy way in.

If you go, go in daylight and take the roads seriously. The pines are flat and look identical in every direction, and people get turned around out there every year. Also, if you hear something screaming at dusk, remember it's probably a fox and keep walking.

faq.q: Where is the Jersey Devil located?
faq.a: The New Jersey Pine Barrens, mainly around Leeds Point in Atlantic County and the forests of Burlington, Camden and Ocean counties. The 1909 sightings spread across South Jersey, Philadelphia, Delaware and western Maryland, so people have reported it well outside the pines.

There's no evidence of an animal. No body, no photo that holds up, no remains. Historians think the name started with the Leeds family and colonial politics, and the familiar winged description was locked in by a week of newspaper panic in January 1909. The sightings themselves are real enough, in the sense that people reported them.

faq.q: Where did the Mother Leeds story come from?
faq.a: There was a real Leeds family at Leeds Point, and Japhet Leeds's 1736 will names twelve children, which fits the thirteenth child story. Historian Brian Regal argues the devil reputation grew from the family's quarrels with local Quakers, an accusation that Daniel Leeds worked for the devil, and Benjamin Franklin publicly treating his son Titan Leeds as a ghost in their almanac feud.

faq.q: Did schools really close during the Jersey Devil panic?
faq.a: Yes, several did during the week of January 16 to 23, 1909, and some mills and businesses let workers stay home. Armed groups went into the pines to hunt it. The Philadelphia Zoo's $10,000 reward is usually reported as an offer made at the time, and it brought out hoaxes including a kangaroo with fake wings.

faq.q: Why is the New Jersey hockey team called the Devils?
faq.a: The franchise moved from Colorado in 1982 and took the name New Jersey Devils after the Pine Barrens legend. It's the most profitable thing the creature has ever done.
